I           Introduction

[
1
]

A tribunal under the
Alberta Human Rights Act
,
R.S.A. 2000, c. A-25.5, decided that Webber Academy unlawfully discriminated
against two high school students by prohibiting them from performing prescribed
forms of prayer on campus. The students, in grades nine and ten, sought to
perform their prayers in private.  They testified that according to their
personal Sunni religious beliefs, the prayers were mandatory, at least during
parts of the school year, during times they were on campus.

[
2
]

This decision arises out of an appeal, not a
rehearing, of the human rights complaints. It therefore involves a review of
how the tribunal framed the issues to be decided, what factual findings it made
on the evidence, what legal tests it identified as governing the issues before
it, and whether it reasonably applied those tests to the evidence.

[
3
]

The two students who are the subject of the
complaints will usually be referred to simply as “the students” and the term
“complainants” will typically refer to the students and their mothers, who have
been involved on their behalf throughout the incidents and pursuit of the
complaints.

II         Complaints

[
4
]

Ms. Farhat Amir and Dr. Shabnam Nazar, on behalf
of their fourteen-year-old sons Sarmad Amir and Naman Siddique, submitted
identical complaints to the Alberta Human Rights Commission on February 13,
2012. On the forms they indicated that they were complaining about Webber
Academy in the area of goods, services or facilities, on the ground of
religious beliefs.

[
5
]

The details were set out in an attached
document. Paraphrased, it may be summarized as follows:

(a)

The students are Sunni Muslims, required to pray
five times a day. At least one of these prayers, and no more than two
(depending upon the time of year), must be performed during school hours.

(b)

They were admitted to Webber Academy on December
1, 2011, and until December 17 their prayers were facilitated by members of
teaching staff and non-teaching staff in empty offices and classrooms.

(c)

On Saturday, December 17, their mothers received
telephone calls from Dr. Neil Webber, President and Chairman, informing them
that prayer was forbidden on the school’s campus.

(d)

In meetings on December 19 and 21, the parents
proposed a number of venues on campus where the children might pray without
anyone seeing them. Dr. Webber, however, would only allow them to remain on
campus if they prayed without bowing or kneeling.

(e)

A final meeting occurred on January 25, 2012,
when the parents said they were simply seeking a space that would accommodate the
children to stand, bow and kneel safely – not dedicated prayer space. No more
than five minutes would be required for each prayer. They were told they would
have to leave the property if they wished to carry out their prayers. Dr.
Webber explained that he did not mind meditation or non-descript prayer, but
bowing and kneeling was too overt.

(f)

The parents responded with a formal written
request for accommodation on February 3, 2012. In response, Dr. Webber refused
to provide the requested accommodations, and stated that because the policies
and procedures of the school had been ignored, the students would not be
accepted for enrollment the following year.

[
6
]

Webber Academy submitted a response, which may
be summarized as follows:

(a)

It is a non-denominational school, fostering an
atmosphere where those of many faiths and cultures would feel equally at home.
This meant that Webber Academy “is not a place where religious activities are
to be carried out by members of any religious group on campus.”

(b)

In pre-admission discussions, Ms. Diane Lever,
Director of Admission, advised the students’ mothers “that Webber Academy was a
non-denominational school and as such we would not be able to accommodate their
request for a prayer space.”

(c)

The problem of prayer space arose again during a
school tour which led to the parties exchanging positions and, ultimately,
notification that the students would not be able to pray on campus and would
not be able to enroll for the following school year.

III        Alberta Human Rights
Act

[
7
]

The complaints were submitted and the tribunal’s
decision was made pursuant to the
Alberta Human Rights Act
.
Thus, the tribunal’s
decision and this appeal are governed by the relevant provisions of that
Act
.

[
8
]

Section 4 protects individuals from discrimination
in the area of goods, services, accommodations or facilities on grounds of
religious beliefs. It provides as follows:

4          No person shall

(a)        deny to any person or class of
persons any goods, services, accommodation or facilities that are customarily
available to the public, or

(b)        discriminate against any person
or class of persons with respect to any goods, services, accommodation or
facilities that are customarily available to the public,

because of the race, religious beliefs,
colour, gender, gender identity, gender expression, physical disability, mental
disability, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, source of income, family
status or sexual orientation of that person or class of persons or of any other
person or class of persons.

Notwithstanding section 4, the
Act
provides
for limited exceptions. Section 11 states as follows:

A contravention of this Act shall be deemed
not to have occurred if the person who is alleged to have contravened the Act
shows that the alleged contravention was reasonable and justifiable in the
circumstances.

[
9
]

Where a contravention of section 4 is found, the
tribunal has broad remedial powers, set out in section 32, as follows:

Section 32 (1) A human rights tribunal

(a) shall, if it finds that a complaint is
without merit, order that the complaint may be dismissed, and

(b) may, if it finds that a complaint has
merit in whole or in part, order the person against whom the finding was made
to do any or all of the following:

(i)         to cease the contravention
complained of;

(ii)        to refrain in the future from
committing the same or any similar contravention;

(iii)       to make available to the person
dealt with contrary to this Act the rights, opportunities or privileges that
person was denied contrary to this Act;

(iv)       to compensate the person dealt
with contrary to this Act for all or any part of any wages or income lost or
expenses incurred by reason of the contravention of this Act;

(v)        to take any other action the tribunal
considers proper to place the person dealt with contrary to this Act in the
position the person would have been in but for the contravention of this Act.

(2)        A human rights tribunal may make
any order as to costs that it considers appropriate.

...

[
10
]

Finally, a tribunal’s decision is subject to an
appeal to this court, as provided in section 37:

37(1)    A party to a proceeding before a
human rights tribunal may appeal an order of the tribunal to the Court of
Queen’s Bench by application filed with the clerk of the Court at the judicial
centre closest to the place where the proceeding was held.

. . .

37(4)    The Court may

(a) confirm, reverse or vary the order of
the human rights tribunal and make any order that the tribunal may make under
section 32, or

(b) remit the matter back to the tribunal
with directions.

...

[
11
]

A tribunal, consisting of one or more members of
the Alberta Human Rights Commission, may be appointed to deal with the
complaint (section 27). In this case, a three-person tribunal was appointed. In
most cases, as here, the director of the Commission has carriage of the
proceeding (section 29), although the complainants are also parties who are
entitled to appear and be represented by counsel (section 30).

IV        Tribunal Decision

[
12
]

The present proceeding is an appeal from the tribunal’s
decision, not a new hearing. Thus, it is important to have close regard to what
the tribunal decided and its reasons.

[
13
]

After an introduction and overview of the
positions of the director (adopted by the complainants) and Webber Academy, the
tribunal focused extensively on “framing the analysis” and making initial
findings. A central issue was whether, as submitted by Webber Academy, the
complainants were seeking a designated prayer space or a space dedicated only
to prayer; or, as the director and complainants argued, the request was for the
students to be able to pray, with flexibility in where that occurred.

[
14
]

The tribunal referred to the complainant’s form
of prayer as described by the student Mr. Siddique. It involved raising his
hands over his head, going into a bowing position, standing up again, going
into prostration (putting his hands on the floor, his knees on the floor, and
his head on the floor), going into a sitting position, going back into prostration,
and then coming back up and standing – all while reciting a number of phrases
and quotations from the
Qur’an
in Arabic. This constituted one unit of
prayer, and four units were required. At the very end, instead of standing up
again, he sat back down, recited a short supplication, and then ended the
prayer. The sequence took five to ten minutes.

[
15
]

The tribunal accepted evidence from Dr. Nazar
that Dr. Webber stated he did not want a visible prayer, but making a cross in
the corner would be okay. A Webber Academy witness distinguished between
wearing a religious “symbol” such as a turban, which was acceptable as a state
of being; and prayer, which was a visible activity that required prayer space.

[
16
]

The tribunal rejected Webber Academy’s framing
of the issue as a request for “prayer space,” observing that the space required
was only slightly larger than the space required to be occupied by a person,
and about the same as sitting in a chair. It did not accept a distinction of
any significance between a visible religious practice or a visible religious
symbol.  It found the complainants were requesting Webber Academy to allow them
to honour their religious beliefs regarding prayer.

[
17
]

The tribunal described a conflict in the
evidence relating to discussions at pre-enrollment meetings. Dianne Lever,
Director of Admissions, testified that she told the parents and students that
the school was non-denominational, therefore no prayer space would be allowed;
Vicki Grenier, Admissions Assistant, testified to overhearing this statement.
Her evidence was said to be of little assistance, because she was not present
for the entire discussion. The students’ mothers said they were told prayers at
school would not be a problem, and Mr. Siddique recalled a similar response.

[
18
]

The students began attending classes on December
1, 2011. On December 13, their mothers were given a tour during which,
according to Dr. Nazar’s testimony, she asked Ms. Lever to thank the teachers
for providing a place to pray, to which Ms. Lever responded “don’t thank me,
thank the teachers.” Ms. Lever testified that her response was “don’t thank me
because I didn’t give permission.” She also testified that a request for space
to pray was not really brought up on the tour, and only in reflecting
afterwards did she realize that Dr. Nazar was looking around for places to
pray.

[
19
]

The tribunal reviewed Ms. Lever’s testimony,
noting her uncertainty about how she might respond to certain religious
practices.  The tribunal found this reduced the reliability of her evidence
about communicating with the parents, and further stated that “Ms. Lever’s lack
of clarity about how to handle a visible religious practice, even now, coupled
with the inconsistencies in her testimony support our conclusion that Ms. Lever
did not clearly articulate or convey that prayer was not allowed at the time
the requests were raised.” They found the testimony of the students and their
mothers to be “more accurate and reliable and consistent with the balance of
the evidence as a whole.” In summary, they found the students’ need to pray was
discussed with Ms. Lever prior to enrollment and a generally positive
indication of acceptance was given, and that on the tour Ms. Lever indicated a
spot in the library where the students could pray.

[
20
]

On December 17, 2011, Dr. Webber telephoned the
parents to say the school was “non-denominational” and the students could not
pray on school premises. The tribunal found that this was the first clear
communication from Webber Academy that the students could not pray on campus.

[
21
]

The students’ parents testified that in
subsequent meetings Dr. Webber refused to allow prayer in private areas such as
an outside garage, corridor, basement, behind trees or a closet. Instead, the
students would have to go off campus. They testified that he suggested students
could pray quietly in their head or quickly make a cross if no one was aware of
the prayer, but did not want other children to see bowing or kneeling.

[
22
]

In correspondence, the parents requested a “nominal
space being provided to perform prayers” and permission to be excused from
class if necessary. A dedicated prayer space was not necessary to meet the
requirements. However, they could not accept a requirement that the children
leave campus to pray, as it would require a disproportionate amount of time and
was potentially dangerous, especially during inclement weather.

[
23
]

Dr. Webber responded in correspondence,
reminding the parents that at the time of admission, they were told by Ms.
Lever “that we are a non-denominational school and as such we would not be able
to accommodate space for prayers.” He referred to a legal opinion that Webber
Academy was under no obligation to accommodate their request, because it does
not make physical accommodations for any other student to practice religion,
and Webber Academy is a non-denominational school, an integral part of its
character. He reiterated that there was no permission to have prayer space at
Webber Academy, and since the policies and procedures were being ignored, the
students would not be accepted for enrollment the following school year.

[
24
]

There was an incident on February 10, 2012 when
Mr. Siddique was praying in the library. He was about to commence prostration
when he was interrupted by Ms. Webber, Vice President of Administration, who
asked repeatedly “what are you doing?” He was upset by the incident. Ms.  Webber
testified that she heard Mr. Siddique praying, and interrupted him to ask what
he was doing and see if he was all right.

[
25
]

The tribunal found that Ms. Webber abruptly
interrupted a quiet prayer. It acknowledged that Mr. Siddique was praying in
violation of a directive, but was attempting to fulfill his religious
obligations as he understood them. In its view, the manner of physical
intrusion and interruption contributed to a sense of shame and humiliation.

[
26
]

The tribunal then turned to consider how to
characterize the relevant “services” and “public” in this case, within the
meaning of the provision that no person shall deny to or discriminate against
any person with respect to services, accommodation or facilities that are
customarily available to the public (my paraphrase of section 4 of the
Act
).
The tribunal defined “the service and facility customarily offered by Webber
Academy to include: educational programs and other supportive services and
facilities including the use of Webber Academy campus and facilities” (para 49)
and defined the “public” as the “student body.” It was significant to the tribunal,
when considering the scope of service and facility, that the students were
minors and attended for full days, thus being dependent upon the school to meet
their needs throughout the day.

[
27
]

Accordingly, the tribunal rejected Webber
Academy’s argument that it did not fall under the
Act
because prayer space
is not a service it customarily makes available to its public. The tribunal
emphasized that prayer space was not the service being offered. Rather, the
service was education and other supportive services and facilities allowing
meaningful access to education.

[
28
]

The tribunal then addressed the evidence of the
students, their mothers and some religious advisers, finding that the students
and their parents had a sincerely held religious belief that their practice of
prayer, at the times requested, was a requirement of their religion. It
rejected Webber Academy’s expert evidence indicating that exceptions during
school attendance were well recognized in Islamic law, and arguments that
certain current and historical practices of the students and their parents
raised questions about the sincerity of their beliefs.

[
29
]

In applying its determination of how to frame
the issue and its factual findings, the tribunal found that there was a
prima
facie
discrimination contrary to section 4 of the
Act
, because:

(a)

The students’ desire to pray during school hours
was based on a sincerely religious belief;

(b)

The students were not allowed to pray on campus
and were refused re-enrollment to Webber Academy, thus experiencing an adverse
impact with respect to the educational services and related facilities of
Webber Academy; and

(c)

Their religious belief, a protected
characteristic under the
Act
, was the basis for Webber Academy’s denial
of services and discrimination with respect to its services.

[
30
]

Having found
prima facie
discrimination,
the tribunal turned to whether it was reasonable and justifiable, thus giving a
defence under section 11 of the
Act
. That involved consideration of
whether “Webber Academy adopted the standard for a purpose or goal that is
rationally connected to the function being performed,” whether it “adopted the
standard in good faith, in the belief that it is necessary for the fulfillment
of the purpose or goal,” and whether the standard was “reasonably necessary” to
accomplish its purpose or goal, in the sense that the defendant cannot
accommodate persons with the characteristics of the claimant without incurring
undue hardship.

[
31
]

With little analysis, the tribunal accepted that
Webber Academy met the first two requirements. However, it failed on the third,
because there was no evidence that the students’ prayer practices would be a
religious influence on other students, other overt religious observances were
permitted, initial allowance of prayers had been easily accommodated, and
Webber Academy had not undertaken any assessment of whether allowing the
students’ prayers would amount to a hardship for Webber Academy.

[
32
]

The tribunal awarded Mr. Amir $12,000 and Mr.
Siddique $14,000 as damages for distress, injury and loss of dignity. Some
factors considered were the tribunal’s finding that Webber Academy had given
the impression before enrollment that something could be worked out regarding
the prayer requirements, and that within three weeks of enrollment, the
students were forbidden to pray on campus, causing them significant upset and
feelings of humiliation.

V         Standard of Review

[
33
]

Principles of administrative law, reformulated
and simplified in
Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick
,
2008 SCC 9
, [2008] 1 S.C.R.
190, and numerous decisions interpreting and applying it, apply to statutory appeals
as well as applications for judicial review:
Mouvement laἵque
québécois v. Saguenay (City),
2015 SCC 16
, 382 D.L.R. (4th) 385, para.
38
.
The tribunal is a specialized administrative body, with expertise. That is
because the legislature has conferred on it decision-making authority on a
particular, assigned subject matter:
Alberta (Information and Privacy
Commissioner) v. Alberta Teacher’s Association
,
2011 SCC 61
, [2011] 3
S.C.R. 654, para.
1
;
Nor-Man Regional Health Authority Inc v. Manitoba
Association of Healthcare Professionals
,
2011 SCC 59
, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 616,
para.
53
. In addition, the tribunal’s expertise can be seen from its
composition. All members must possess a law degree and experience, knowledge or
training in human rights or administrative law: Commission
Bylaws
,
section 13 (3), passed pursuant to section 17 (1) of the
Act.

[
34
]

The standards of review that apply to various
questions on appeal were succinctly set out by Ross J. in
Association of
Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta v. Mihaly
,
2016 ABQB
61
. I can do no better than set out her statement of the standards, which I respectfully
adopt:

[48]      Questions of procedural fairness
are reviewed on the basis of whether the proceedings met the level of fairness
required by law:
Wright v. College and Association of Registered Nurses of
Alberta (Appeals Committee)
,
2012 ABCA 267
at para.
31
, 355 DLR (4th) 197 .
. . .

[49]      Questions of law concerning the
interpretation of the
Alberta Human Rights Act
, RSA 2000, c A-25.5 . . .
are reviewed for reasonableness, unless they are “of central importance to the
legal system and fall outside the adjudicator’s specialized area of expertise”:

Saguenay
at paras. 46-48.

[50]      The test for
prima facia

discrimination is reviewed on the correctness standard:
Stewart
[
Stewart
v. Elk Valley Coal Corporation
,
2015 ABCA 225
] at paras. 47, 56-57, citing
Saguenay

at paras. 46-48.

[51]      A lack of evidence in the record
to support a Tribunal’s decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard:
Bombardier

[
Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse)
v. Bombardier Inc.,
2015 SCC 39
]. ...

VI Characterizations: Students’ Request and Services
Customarily Available

[
35
]

Section 4 of the
Act
, quoted in its
entirety earlier and paraphrased in its essential elements here, states that no
person shall deny to any person, or discriminate against any person with
respect to, any services or facilities that are customarily available to the
public, because of religious beliefs.

[
36
]

The parties agree that, as in
Berg v.
University of British Columbia
,
1993 CanLII 89 (SCC)
, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 353, 102 D.L.R. (4th) 665,
here the “public” for section 4 purposes is the student body of Webber Academy.
The difference concerns whether there was a denial of or discrimination with
respect to any services or facilities “customarily available to the public.”
Resolving that issue requires characterizing what the students were seeking and
how that relates to the services offered to Webber Academy’s student body – its
“public.”

[
37
]

The tribunal rejected as factually inaccurate
Webber Academy’s characterization of the students’ request as being for “prayer
space” (para. 20). It found that the space required for the requested prayer
was “only slightly larger than the space occupied by a person,” and about the
same as if the person were sitting in a chair. The tribunal’s characterization
was that the students “were requesting Webber Academy allow them to honour
their religious beliefs regarding their prayer” (para. 20).

[
38
]

Determining what was requested by the students
is primarily a factual matter and thus reviewable on a reasonableness standard.
There was evidence to support the tribunal’s finding on this point. In addition
to the express basis for its finding, there was evidence that the students were
willing to perform their prayers in any private place, such as an unused room
or behind a tree outside. While the complainants occasionally used the term
“prayer space,” there was ample evidence on which the tribunal could find that
they were not seeking dedicated space – only somewhere they could perform
prayers for five to ten minutes in an unobtrusive way. In other words, they
wanted permission to go somewhere to pray privately for a few minutes, and that
place could be different from time to time.

[
39
]

It must then be determined whether what the
students requested was a service or facility customarily available to the
Webber Academy public, which means determining what Webber Academy offers to
the student body. The tribunal took a broad view: “[t]his Tribunal defines the
service and facility customarily offered by Webber Academy to include:
educational programs and other supportive services and facilities including the
use of Webber Academy campus and facilities” (para. 49).

[
40
]

In this appeal, Webber Academy does not
articulate clearly how its services and facilities should be described. Its
focus, rather, is on arguing that the applicable service to be considered is
what the students were requesting, namely the provision of prayer space,
something that was never “customarily” available because it had never been
offered to any segment of the student body. In effect, Webber Academy argues
that if the specific thing requested is not customarily available to the
student body, it is not within the requirements of section 4 of the
Act
.

[
41
]

For its approach, Webber Academy relies on
portions of 1984 and 1986 Queen’s Bench decisions and 1990 and 2011 decisions
from, respectively, an individual sitting as a board of inquiry under the
Individual’s
Rights Protection Act
, R.S.A. 1980 c.I-2, and the British Columbia Human
Rights Tribunal, respectively. However, the Supreme Court of Canada has set out
clearly the required approach in
Berg

and
Moore v. British Columbia
(Ministry of Education)
,
2012 SCC 61
, 351 D.L.R. (4th) 451. The tribunal
was correct in using those cases to guide its approach to interpreting section
4 and applying it to the case before it.

[
42
]

In
Berg
, which involved a complainant’s
participation in a master’s program in nutrition, the court noted that the
“School exists to provide accommodations, services or facilities to its
students which will further their education and social activities relating to
the School” (para. 64). The complainant developed an emotional instability
after her admission to the program, on the basis of which the director denied
her a key for after-hours access to the school building and a faculty member
refused to complete a rating sheet to support her application for a dietetic
internship at a hospital. The court found that the school facilities were part
of the relationship between the university and its students, since they were a
necessary adjunct to the educational process, and thus the key was likened to
the educational and recreational services of the school generally: (para. 66).
Similarly, the rating sheet (in effect, much like a transcript) was an incident
of the educational relationship between faculty and students: (para. 67). “The
key and rating sheet,” held the Court, “were incidents of this public
relationship between the School and its students” (para.78).

[
43
]

In
Moore
, the complainant was a learning
disabled student who was enrolled in a public school system. For financial
reasons, the specialized intensive remediation which he required was no longer
available. The Court held that, under a section equivalent to section 4 of our
Act
,
the “service” was education generally, and the special education required by
the complainant was the means by which students with learning disabilities
could get meaningful access to the general education services available to the
public served by the respondent. (paras. 26 to 29).

[
44
]

Analogously, in this case the services and
facilities Webber Academy customarily made available to its public were
non-denominational educational programs and other supportive services and
facilities incidental to those programs – or to use the language of
Moore
,
the means by which those programs could be accessed by students. As in
Berg
,
Webber Academy has a discretion in the types and scope of incidental services
and facilities it offers. Examples could be the types of sporting events, hours
of access to facilities and the range of courses taught. However, the
discretion must not be exercised on prohibited grounds of discrimination:
Berg
,
para.
75
.

[
45
]

Thus, the tribunal was correct in concluding
“that Webber Academy, as a private school, offers services and facilities
customarily available to the public and does not have an ‘unfettered
discretion’ to summarily refuse a student’s request to perform a religious
obligation on its campus”. Webber Academy’s discretion to set policies
regarding student conduct “does not give a private school license to exercise
their discretion in denying the services or use of facilities in a
discriminatory fashion” (para. 51).

[
46
]

Further, to define the services and facilities
addressed in section 4 of the
Act
as proposed by Webber Academy – that
is, to define them as identical to the specific “service” requested by the
students – would make the provision almost meaningless. A respondent could refuse
any request because it does not “customarily” provide it. So, for example, a
school could say it will not provide wheelchair access for facilities to
someone with a physical disability: it has never done so before, and thus it is
not something customarily available to its public. Equating the services and
facilities customarily available to the public in section 4 with the thing
requested by a complainant simply defines away the issue.

VII
Prima Facie

Discrimination

A.        Introduction

[
47
]

The tribunal applied the three-part test set out
in
Moore
to determine whether there was
prima facie

discrimination; in other words, whether the evidence showed an adverse impact
on the students caused or contributed to on the ground of their religious
beliefs.  If so, Webber Academy would have the burden of proving that its
policy was justifiable.

[
48
]

Webber Academy submitted, both before the tribunal
and on this appeal, that the
Moore
test was inadequate because it failed
to incorporate a “comparator analysis” as used in
Kelly v. B.C. (Ministry of
Public Safety and Solicitor General)
,
2011 BCHRT 183
.

[
49
]

As I will address presently, there is room
within the
Moore
approach for a comparator analysis, although it is
doubtful that it is required. In any event, the tribunal was correct in identifying
the
Moore
test as applicable, being the most recent relevant Supreme
Court of Canada authority. It has been recognized in Alberta as the applicable
test:
Telecommunications Workers Union v. Telus Communications Inc
,
2014
ABCA 154
, [2014] 6 W.W.R. 217, para.
28
;
SMS Equipment Inc v. CEP Local 707
,

2015 ABQB 162
, 18 Alta. L.R. (6th) 74, para.
72
.

[
50
]

Thus, to establish
prima facie

discrimination, it must be shown that:

(a)

The complainant has a characteristic that is
protected from discrimination;

(b)

The complainant has experienced an adverse
impact; and

(c)

The protected characteristic was a factor in the
adverse impact.

B.        Application of the Test

1.         Characteristic
Protected from Discrimination

[
51
]

The tribunal found that the students had a
characteristic protected from discrimination under the
Act
, because of
their sincerely held religious beliefs. Webber Academy disputes this finding,
arguing that “at the very least, the patent inconsistencies between the
Complainants’ stated beliefs and actual practices, contextualized by the expert
evidence of Dr. Ahmed, should have caused the Tribunal to examine whether the
demand for prayer space was in accordance with their sincerely held beliefs” (Brief,
para. 141).

[
52
]

Webber Academy argues that the tribunal gave
inadequate consideration to the expert testimony of Dr. Rumee Ahmed, assistant
professor of Islamic law at the University of British Columbia; that Dr.
Ahmed’s testimony established there was no religious obligation to adhere
strictly to prayer times during school hours, because leading and majority
opinion among the four major Sunni schools of Islamic law consider attendance
at school a valid reason to delay prayer; and that some practices of the
students and their parents show a willingness to skip or miss regular prayer.

[
53
]

The tribunal reasonably considered Dr. Ahmed’s
evidence in detail as part of its determination of whether the students’
practice of prayer in the manner and at the times requested was based on their
sincerely held religious belief (paras. 58 to 68). It also considered the
testimony of the students, their mothers and three members of the Muslim
community: Mahdi Qasqas, director of youth services in Calgary, who had become
a mentor for the students; Imam Fayaz Tilli, a Calgary imam and a religious
leader with the Muslim council in Calgary; and Birju Dattani, a PhD student,
legal academic and non-practicing barrister living in London England (involved
in the Calgary Muslim community while growing up, and a close friend of Mr. Qasqas).
Messrs Qasqas and Dattani attended one of the meetings between the students’
mothers and Webber Academy staff.

[
54
]

However, the essence of the tribunal’s decision
on religious beliefs was based upon its finding that the students personally
believed it was necessary to conduct their prayers during scheduled times and
it would be sinful to regularly miss them. The students, as accepted by the tribunal,
believed that their obligations come from the
Qur’an
and the sayings of
the Prophet as conveyed to them by their parents – recognizing that at the
relevant time, the students were in grades nine and ten respectively. It found
that Dr. Ahmed’s opinion did not establish that the students could miss prayers
without consequence to their personal and sincerely held religious beliefs and
obligations, and that nothing in his opinion challenged the sincerity of belief
of the students or their parents.

[
55
]

In addition to accepting the evidence of the
students, the tribunal accepted the testimony of the principal of Rundle
College, where the students attended after Webber Academy, that the students
practiced their prayer without significant disruption for the two years they
attended his school. The tribunal considered this strong evidence of a genuine
belief and commitment by the students to their prayer practices.

[
56
]

Thus, the tribunal rejected arguments based on
the contention that there were many valid schools of thought within Islamic law
that would have permitted the students to miss or delay their prayers, and
instead focused on the personal beliefs of the students. In doing so, the tribunal
correctly followed the approach established in
Syndicat Northcrest v.
Amselem
,
2004 SCC 47
, 241 D.L.R. (4th) 1. As Webber Academy notes,
Amselem

addressed freedom of religion under the
Quebec
Charter of Human Rights and
Freedoms
and the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. Webber
Academy argued that therefore it should not be applied to this case. However,
Amselem
’s
mandated approach to determining what religious beliefs are protected applies
with equal force to the
Act
here. None of the distinctions between the
Charters

and the
Act
make a difference on that point.

[
57
]

Amselem
holds
that for complainants relying upon freedom of religion, it is not necessary to
prove  their beliefs are objectively recognized as valid by coreligionists.
Nor is it appropriate for courts to inquire into that question; rather, a
person must show sincerity of belief, not validity of a particular belief: para
43. Courts are not arbiters of scriptural interpretation, or responsible for
making decisions among competing doctrines: paras 44 through 46.

[
58
]

“This approach to freedom of religion,” stated
the court, “effectively avoids the invidious interference of the State and its
courts with religious belief. The alternative would undoubtedly result in . . .
value-judgment indictments of those beliefs that may be unconventional or not
mainstream” (para. 55). The
Amselem
approach is sound, and even more
important as society becomes increasingly diverse and secular. What were once
mainstream religious beliefs and practices often have become minority positions.

[
59
]

In my view, the tribunal correctly focused on a
determination of whether the students sincerely held their religious beliefs
regarding the form and times of prayer. There was ample evidence from the
students, their mothers and their coreligionists to support the tribunal’s
finding that the religious beliefs were sincerely held.

[
60
]

Finally,
Amselem
does not support the
reliance placed by Webber Academy on expert evidence. It is open to a
complainant to adduce expert evidence, the court held, to demonstrate consistency
of belief with the practices and beliefs of other adherents, as this may be
relevant to a demonstration of sincerity. However, it is not necessary. In the
words of the court, “[r]eligious belief is intensely personal and can easily
vary from one individual to another. Requiring proof of the established
practices of a religion to gauge the sincerity of belief diminishes the very
freedom we seek to protect” (para. 54).

2.         Adverse Impact

[
61
]

The tribunal found that the students suffered an
adverse impact with respect to the services and facilities denied by Webber
Academy, by not being allowed to pray on campus and being refused re-enrollment
for the following school year.

[
62
]

Webber Academy does not seriously challenge this
finding, although in another context submits that differential treatment must
be established to prove
prima facie
discrimination under the
Act.
As
noted earlier, this is not expressly required as a consideration under the
Moore

test, but the argument can be addressed as part of the question of whether
the students experienced an adverse impact with respect to the service or
facility.

[
63
]

Webber Academy’s argument was expressed as
follows:

Simply put, the impugned non-denominational
policy demands the same respect for a non-sectarian environment from every
student, regardless of their belief system. Second, the service sought by the
Complainants, namely prayer space, is not available to any student of Webber
Academy. The Tribunal’s Decision effectively compels Webber Academy to provide
a benefit for the exclusive enjoyment of the Complainants. Webber Academy did
not refuse admission to the school and did not prevent the Complainants from
accessing the service it does make available to its students: the provision of
an education and a place in which to absorb that education. It further agreed
they could take time off from class if needed. However, prayer space cannot be
conceptualized as a requirement of this education. [Brief, para. 111.]

[
64
]

Webber Academy’s argument is premised on a mistaken
characterization of the issues, as addressed earlier. The students wanted to be
allowed to conduct private prayers of a few minutes in length, in whatever
unobtrusive place was available, because they considered this necessary to follow
their religion while attending school for complete days. It would give them
meaningful access to the education and facilities which Webber Academy
customarily made available to its student body. In being denied their right to
pray, they were being treated differently from other students whose religious
beliefs in the form of head coverings and facial hair were permitted during
their attendance at school, even advertised by Webber Academy, despite the fact
that those observances were contrary to the usual policies applicable to Webber
Academy students.

[
65
]

Thus, while the tribunal was not required to
address the question of whether there was differential treatment, there was
ample evidence showing that differential treatment existed.

3.         Religious Belief a Factor
in Adverse Impact

[
66
]

Finally, the tribunal found that the students
were denied services, namely re-enrollment and the ability to exercise their
religious prayer on campus.  These denials were based on the students’
religious beliefs, which clearly connects the protected ground of religion to
the adverse impacts of refusal to allow prayer and denial of enrollment: para.
79.

[
67
]

In summarizing its conclusions, and paraphrasing

Moore
, the tribunal found that
prima facie
discrimination had
been established, because “[a]fter having met all of the eligibility and
admission requirements . . ., the Students were thereafter denied
meaningful

access
to Webber Academy (in all its facility and service offerings)
based on their religious belief, a protected ground” (para. 81, original
emphasis).

[
68
]

This was a reasonable finding based on the
evidence.

VIII     Reasonable Justification

A.        Introduction

[
69
]

Having found
prima facie
discrimination,
the tribunal considered whether, to paraphrase section 11 of the
Act
, a
contravention should be deemed not to have occurred because Webber Academy
established the
prima facie
discrimination was reasonable and
justifiable in the circumstances.

[
70
]

To address whether Webber Academy met its onus
of establishing this defence, the tribunal correctly identified the test as the
one set out in
British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles) v.
British Columbia (Counsel of Human Rights)
,
1999 CanLII 646 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 868 (commonly
known as “
Grismer,”
the name of the claimant and appellant). The test in

Grismer
is as follows:

Once the plaintiff established that the
standard is
prima facie
discriminatory, the onus shifts to the defendant
to prove on a balance of probabilities that the discriminatory standard is a
BFOR [
bona fide
occupational requirement] or has a bona fide and
reasonable justification. In order to establish this justification, the
defendant must prove that:

(1)        it adopted the
standard for a purpose or goal that is rationally connected to the function
being performed;

(2)        it adopted the
standard in good faith, in the belief that it is necessary for the fulfillment
of the purpose or goal; and

(3)        the standard is
reasonably necessary to accomplish its purpose or goal, in the sense that the
defendant cannot accommodate persons with the characteristics of the claimant
without incurring undue hardship. [Para. 20.]

B.        Application of the Test

1.         Rational Connection

[
71
]

The tribunal found that Webber Academy’s
standard, which had evolved (that is, developed in unwritten form, in response to
circumstances), could be expressed as “no overt prayer or religious activities
on school property” (para. 86). The purpose for the standard, as determined by
the tribunal, “was to foster a non-denominational identity that ensures Webber
Academy’s students are placed in a learning environment that is ‘free of
religious influence’ ” (para. 88).

[
72
]

Neither the standard or the purpose was
articulated in any of Webber Academy’s written materials, such as handbooks and
information packages. They were pieced together as the issue with the students
and their mothers developed, and in testimony before the tribunal. Thus, they
were developed in an
ad hoc
way to deal with a specific problem that
arose.

[
73
]

Having identified the standard and the purpose,
the tribunal then identified the “function being performed” as educational
services and facilities, and observed that a school could create an identity
that includes setting standards for the conduct of students and staff “in the
particular learning environment and on its campus” (para. 90).

[
74
]

It concluded by finding that Webber Academy had
established a rational connection between Webber Academy’s purpose and the
function it performed, noting that the standard’s validity is not addressed at
this stage (para. 90). This finding is not challenged.

2.         Good Faith

[
75
]

The tribunal readily found that Webber Academy
had adopted its position in good faith, thus meeting the second element of the
test. Again, this finding is not challenged.

3.         Reasonably Necessary

[
76
]

Finally, the tribunal considered whether the
standard (of no overt prayer or religious activities on campus) was reasonably
necessary to accomplish its purpose of fostering a non-denominational identity.

[
77
]

At various times in its decision, the tribunal
referred to the few written references to religion that appeared in Webber
Academy’s public information. It will be helpful to collect them here:

(a)

The
Parent-Student Handbook
stated on its
first page that “Webber Academy is a non-denominational, co-educational,
university preparatory school offering Junior Kindergarten to Grade 12.” On
page six, it stated that “at Webber Academy, we believe in,” among other
things, “creating an atmosphere where young people of many faiths and cultures
feel equally at home.” At page 24 of the same document, it is stated that “head
coverings which have a cultural or religious significance are permitted and may
be worn,” but other head wear may not be worn in the building at any time. Page
23 stated that “boys are to be clean-shaven.”

(b)

On Webber Academy’s website page for
“Admissions,” a student with a turban, mustache and beard was prominently
shown, along with two other students, thus conveying the acceptance of students
of many backgrounds and faiths.

(c)

In a statement on “our beliefs and values” from
the website, the board and school faculty were stated to believe in “creating
an atmosphere where young people of many faiths and cultures feel equally at
home.” There followed a list of what is expected from students, such as respect
for others, being truthful and honest, being courteous, and so forth. After
this list of virtues, the document closed with the words “these are timeless
values, honoured by all the world’s great religions. They are essential to
becoming a whole person, developing integrity and building lasting relations
with others.”

(d)

The “Webber Academy information package” also
contained the statement that Webber Academy is “non-denominational.”

[
78
]

When questioned about how one would know that
prayer was not allowed at Webber Academy, Dr. Webber testified that it was
“because it is reflected in our parent/student handbook that we’re a
non-denominational school” (quoted in decision, para. 93). Ms. Webber defined
the term “non-denominational” as providing students with “an academic
atmosphere that does not include a religious practice” and “it’s a place where
you don’t have students conform to any one belief or prefer one belief or
another” (para. 96).

[
79
]

The tribunal referred to a dictionary definition
of “non-denominational” as “not restricted to or associated with a religious
denomination,” and accepted a statement given by the principal of Rundle
College who defined non-denominational as “we are not promoting or specifically
affiliated with any denomination” (para. 97). It did not accept Dr. Webber’s
view that a non-denominational school can reasonably be interpreted as meaning
that no prayer or religious practice would be allowed.

[
80
]

The tribunal went on to consider Webber
Academy’s concern that allowing the student’s prayer practices would force
Webber Academy to adopt the view that religious observance belongs in a school
setting.   The tribunal rejected this concern, finding that the students were
not attempting to establish any particular view, but were merely fulfilling
their religious obligation of praying when the time for prayer occurred during
school hours. Further, the tribunal noted that the students were seeking to
pray privately, and that allowing two of nine hundred students to pray behind
closed doors for a few minutes would be insignificant in the context of
religious identity, affiliation or influence.

[
81
]

The tribunal also noted the numerous authorities
recognizing that religion is an integral aspect of a person’s life, and that schools
must allow and accommodate religious observances (such as kirpans and turbans)
despite policies to the contrary. The tribunal found that “[t]he evidence
overwhelmingly supports that accommodation of the prayer was possible and it
would not have been an undue hardship to accommodate the Students’ requests to
pray on campus” (para. 118). In arriving at its conclusion, the tribunal had
reference to the practices of others schools which it found helpful, but not
determinative. It also noted the testimony of Dr. Webber that the school did
not contemplate any hardship aspects – they had a policy which they believed
was important to enforce.

[
82
]

In further support of its finding on undue hardship,
the tribunal noted that four staff members participated in facilitating prayers
for the first two and a half weeks of the students attendance, and that other
overt religious obligations such as the wearing of a turban were permitted as
an exception to school policy.

[
83
]

The tribunal’s findings that the standard
imposed by Webber Academy on the students was not reasonably necessary to
accomplish its purpose of fostering a non-denominational identity were
reasonable, founded on the evidence.

[
84
]

Webber Academy did not seek to justify its
standard on the basis of a financial or logistical hardship. Thus, those are
not a consideration. Its justification on the basis of needing to ensure
consistency with its non-denominational character fails for a number of
reasons.

[
85
]

None of Webber Academy’s explanatory and
promotional material would lead to the conclusion that it sought to exclude all
forms of religious expression from its campus. Rather, it conveyed the message
that it would welcome adherents of all faiths and cultures, including those
whose religious beliefs involved some overt indication of their beliefs.

[
86
]

The students’ prayer practices would be carried
out in private, for short periods. It would usually occur outside of class
times (but if necessary, Webber Academy allowed their absence from class during
prayer time). Thus, these religious practices would be less obvious to staff
and other students than other overt religious observances already permitted,
even welcomed, by Webber Academy.

4.         Conclusions

[
87
]

The tribunal correctly identified the legal
tests to be applied in considering whether a defence under section 11 of the
Act

was made out. The standard for applying that test on the case before it is
reasonableness. I am satisfied that the tribunal’s conclusions were reasonable.
There was ample evidence to support its findings.

IX        Evidence of
Pre-Enrollment Meeting and School Tour

A.        Summary of Evidence

[
88
]

Webber Academy argues that the tribunal erred in
dealing with the evidence concerning the pre-enrollment meeting on November 29,
2011 and the December 13, 2013 school tour, primarily in failing to adequately
make and explain findings of credibility.

[
89
]

The November 29, 2011 meeting was attended by
the two students, their mothers, and Ms. Lever, Webber Academy’s Director of Admissions.
Ms. Grenier, Admissions Assistant, was present during parts of the meeting, but
was in and out. Testimony about the meeting was given by all of these
witnesses, except for Mr. Amir.

[
90
]

Ms. Amir and Dr. Nazar testified that they
specially discussed the students’ requirement for space to pray, and were told
by Ms. Lever that it would not be a problem. Mr. Siddique said Ms. Lever said
something to the effect of “we can see if we can work out something,” and
“there probably would be some kind of empty space” where they could pray.

[
91
]

This testimony was squarely contradicted by Ms.
Lever. She testified that Mr. Siddique had attended a classroom visit earlier
that day, after which both mothers requested a further meeting (in addition to
an earlier one on November 10). The meeting was held in Ms. Lever’s office,
with the door open. Ms. Grenier was in and out of the room organizing
application paperwork.

[
92
]

Ms. Lever confirmed that she was asked about
prayer space and “I indicated no, I’m sorry, we are a non-denominational
school, and we would not be able to provide prayer space for their children,
that we have many children of different faiths and cultures at the school, and
they do not receive a spot for prayer. So I indicated that no, we did not have
that” (transcript, 856-857). She further testified that the issue came up
again. Her response was “I had indicated yet again, that, no, we would not be
able to provide prayer space and that, you know, that is something that would
have to be taken into consideration before enrolling the children” (858).

[
93
]

Ms. Lever testified that Ms. Grenier was present
when Dr. Nazar raised the issue of prayer. Mrs. Amir also testified that the
request for prayer space was raised in the presence of Ms. Grenier, although
she testified that Ms. Lever’s response was that there would not be a problem.

[
94
]

Ms. Grenier testified that she heard the request
for prayer space and Ms. Lever’s response that the school was
non-denominational and did not provide prayer space to its students. Further,
she recalled having a conversation with Ms. Lever about the subject after the
meeting, and they “were both quite surprised that the families were asking for
prayer space because we’ve never dealt with the situation before” (895).

[
95
]

On December 13, 2011, Ms. Lever and the two
parents went on a tour of the main school building. Dr. Nazar testified that
she arranged the tour with the intent of locating space for prayer. During the
tour, she testified to thanking Ms. Lever for providing prayer space, and then
described Ms. Lever’s response as follows:

And then I thanked her for the school
providing the space, and I even said that, Make sure that you thank the staff
members that they’re providing this facility. I mean, they’re providing the
space for the kids to pray. And she said, Don’t thank me. You can thank them.
They are the ones who are doing it. And I said, Sure. But, of course, you know,
as a school, I said, Thank you very much. And during that meeting, she said,
What about here in the library? And she pointed out like that to a corner and
said, What about in that corner? Can they pray there? And I said, yeah,
absolutely. That’s actually a very good idea. When there is nobody around, they
can pray there, otherwise an empty classroom or anything. And she said, yeah,
okay. [147]

Ms. Amir, although a witness, did
not testify about any discussions during the tour regarding prayer.

[
96
]

Ms. Lever, again, gave very different testimony.
She observed that the tour was unusual, as the students had already been attending
for about two weeks, and the parents were not asking questions about
facilities, curriculum or teaching methodology. Her testimony on whether there
was discussion about prayer space was as follows:

Q.        Okay. What was discussed about
prayer space?

A.        It
really wasn’t brought up outright. On the tour, I remember, in the library,
Shabnam Nazar was looking arounds corners and in behind bookshelves and – and,
you know, may have commented about that there might be a spot to pray. And I
had indicated again, no, we do not provide prayer space. And she thanked me for
providing prayer space; I said well, don’t thank me because I did not give
permission for this. And I then questioned where this was being done, and who
had given them permission, because I had clearly indicated prior to enrollment
that we would not be able to provide this for them. And, so, it was a shock to
me. I was very surprised that someone would be thanking me for something that I
had clearly indicated “no” to.

And at that time,
I do believe that I brought up that we have many people of many faiths and
cultures at the school, students and staff, and that we have a – you know, a
head of school who is Jewish, for example, who must leave the school on
occasion to fulfill her religious requirements. So I was giving – I was
reiterating that it is not provided for anyone, not even staff members at the
school.

And
– and I was just in shock. And the tour ended and then I went immediately to
our administrative offices and asked if this is something that they knew about
or they were aware of, because I felt, as director of admission, if that was
something someone had given permission for, that I would know about it and I
would have been told, because, again, I’m the first point of contact and should
know these things if I’m touring people.

Q.        At
any time during this tour did you identify places were there could be suitable
prayer space?

A.        No, I didn’t.

Q.        Did
you ask any questions of either of the mothers about their manner of prayer,
how they pray, or anything of that nature?

A.        Never.

Q.        And
you talked about what you did after the tour. I just want to be clear, so how
did the tour end?

A.        That’s
pretty much what I remember. Where it ended is when Dr. Nazar thanked me for
providing prayer space for her children, and I was very surprised and said,
well, don’t thank me, because I did not give permission for this. And I – I
kept quiet because I was surprised and I kept fairly quiet. I wanted to find
out how this came about.

Q.        Okay.
So, then, you identified the next steps that you took, and if you’ve said it,
I’ve forgotten, so I just want to be clear. Who did you speak with after the
tour?

A.        I
believe I went directly into Ms. Barbara Webber’s office, our vice president of
administration. I would have gone directly to Dr. Neil Webber’s office,
however, he would likely have been busy with someone, and – so then I went to
her office.

Q.        And
we know that Dr. Webber called the two families on November 17
th
.
Between the 13
th
and the 17
th
, did you have any further
involvement in this issue?

A.        No.
I left it up to Barb Webber and – and Neil Webber to deal with at that point.
[864-866]

[
97
]

Thus, the tribunal was presented with sharply
conflicting evidence on a point it clearly considered significant, given its
review of the evidence and its findings. At the pre-enrollment meeting, all the
evidence established that there was a discussion about whether the students
could pray on campus. The complainants’ testimony was to the effect that Ms.
Lever assured them it would be allowed, or would not be a problem. Ms. Lever’s
testimony was that she gave a firm refusal, and the matter would have to be
considered further before enrollment. Similar conflicts arise with respect to
the school tour, although Ms. Amir (who was present) gave no testimony about
such a discussion during the tour.

B.        Need for Reasonableness
(Transparency and Intelligibility) in Findings

[
98
]

Ms. Grenier’s evidence strongly corroborated Ms.
Lever’s version of the discussion at the pre-enrollment meeting, which the tribunal
in effect acknowledged. However, it completely disregarded her testimony on the
following basis:

However, she acknowledged she did not hear
the entire conversation because she was in and out of the office. We find Ms.
Grenier’s evidence to be of little assistance in that she was not present for
the entire discussion of the Students’ religious beliefs and prayer requests.
[Para 23.]

That was an unreasonable basis for
setting aside evidence going to the heart of the conflicting testimony the tribunal
sought to resolve. It does not matter whether Ms. Grenier was present for the
entire meeting if she was present for the critical part of the discussion.

[
99
]

The tribunal concluded “that Ms. Lever did not
clearly articulate or convey that prayer was not allowed at the time the
requests were raised” (para. 29), based on what it found to be uncertainty
regarding a relatively straightforward question, which was a hypothetical, thus
lessening the reliability of her evidence. The tribunal’s basis for this
conclusion was as follows:

. . . At the hearing, Ms. Lever was asked
what she would do if she saw someone who was Catholic cross themselves at a
meal or take out their rosary beads while on campus at Webber Academy. She
responded:

I might approach them and ask them what they
are doing. I don’t know. I would have to probably seek administrative
direction, but being the Director of admissions, I don’t normally, you know, go
in and discipline the children because I’m not one of their teachers. So I
don’t really know what I would actually do in that situation because I – I
haven’t been in that situation at school.

Moments earlier Ms. Lever had defined
“non-denominational” as:

“Non-denominational”, to me, meant that we
would welcome children of all different faiths and cultures, that we wouldn’t
have open practices of faith, that that would be something that families would
take care of on – outside of school time, and that our focus would be academic.

If Ms. Lever was clear about Webber
Academy’s school policies on religion it is to be reasonably expected that she
would know what to do when seeing a student visibly display a religious
observance. Her response and uncertainty, with a relatively straightforward
question, highlights her uncertainty and lessens the reliability of her
evidence in relation to her communications with the Parents about Webber
Academy’s policies on religious practices. Ms. Lever initially testified that
her response to being asked to thank the teachers was to ask questions of the
Parents about who was allowing prayer and then offer explanations that not
event staff members can pray on campus. Subsequently, she testified that upon
being asked to thank the teachers she became very quiet and the tour ended. Ms.
Lever’s lack of clarity about how to handle a visible religious practice, even
now, coupled with the inconsistencies in her testimony support our conclusion
that Ms. Lever did not clearly articulate or convey that prayer was not allowed
at the time the requests were raised.

The Students and the Parents were all
consistent in their evidence regarding the initial discussions held. Further,
the Students openly approaching staff and teachers in their first few weeks of
school to enable performing their prayers, is consistent with an understanding
that prayer was acceptable. We find that the Students’ and Parents’ version of
the initial conversations prior to enrollment are more accurate and reliable
and consistent with the balance of the evidence as a whole. By way of summary,
we find the Students’ need to pray was discussed with Ms. Lever prior to
enrollment and a generally positive indication of acceptance was given. We
further find that on the tour, Ms. Lever indicated a spot in the library were
the Students could pray. [Tribunal decision, paras. 27 to 30.]

[
100
]

The tribunal’s explanations for not accepting
Ms. Lever’s evidence, particularly in light of its corroboration by Ms.
Grenier, are unreasonable. Her response to the hypothetical question about
Catholics crossing themselves or taking out rosary beads is an honest,
straightforward response, on the spot, to a matter she had never encountered.
By “inconsistency,” the tribunal appears to be referring to Ms. Lever’s
response to Dr. Nazar’s offer of thanks for the students being allowed to pray,
and whether she asked follow-up questions. Ms. Lever’s entire testimony on
these points, reproduced above, displays no inconsistency of any material
nature.

[
101
]

It is doubtful that the first couple of weeks of
school is more consistent with the complainants’ version than Ms. Lever’s. All
that occurred was that the students were being accommodated with places to pray
in a fashion unknown to school administration. Those facts can be squared with
either version of the pre-enrollment meeting and school tour. The tribunal did
not explain why the events corroborated the complainants’ testimony.

[
102
]

As Mahoney J. held in
Syncrude Canada Ltd v.
Saunders
,
2015 ABQB 237
, 26 Alta. L.R (6th) 83, “where there are major
inconsistencies or contradictions with the testimony of key witnesses, or where
there is otherwise conflicting evidence, the trier of fact must carefully asses
the evidence and make credibility findings” (para 43); and “where a finding of
credibility is not properly articulated in a decision-maker’s reasons, the
decision lacks the necessary transparency and intelligibility required in the
decision-making process” (para 48), citing authority on the last point. His
statement of a tribunal’s responsibility finds support in the seminal case of
Dunsmuir
,
where it was held that “[i]n judicial review, reasonableness is concerned
mostly with the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility
within the decision-making process” (para. 47); and in
Telus Communications
Inc v. Telecommunication Workers Union
,
2014 ABCA 199
, 575 A.R. 325, para.

28
.

[
103
]

The tribunal was required to resolve the
inconsistency in testimony, and was entitled to prefer the evidence of the
complainants on grounds that were reasonable, that is, transparent and
intelligent. Here, the tribunal’s reasons for preferring the complainants’
version of pre-enrollment discussions about prayer over the version given by Webber
Academy lacks transparency and intelligibility. Perhaps the tribunal did not
believe that Ms. Lever and Ms. Grenier were truthful in their testimony. If so,
it was required to state that conclusion and give reasons. Or it may have had
other reasons for preferring one version of events over another, but again was
required to articulate those reasons intelligibly.

C.        Effect of Fact Findings on
Finding of Discrimination

[
104
]

I have found that the tribunal failed in its
obligation to provide transparent and intelligible reasons for factual findings
regarding pre-enrollment communications. I must consider whether my conclusions
on this point justify setting aside the tribunal’s decision.

[
105
]

Section 4 of the
Act
allows a remedy
whether the discrimination on prohibited grounds is with respect to denying the
service (for example, refusing admission) or discriminating with respect to the
service (such as not allowing meaningful access to the service or its ancillary
facilities). Thus, if Webber Academy’s evidence were accepted, and the tribunal
found that it had clearly warned the complainants that no prayers could be said
on campus, the tribunal would still have been required, by law, to hold that
Webber Academy had unlawfully discriminated against the students. The law
prevents Webber Academy from adopting, or applying, policies that result in
discrimination on prohibited grounds, unless they can show the discrimination
was reasonable and justifiable.

[
106
]

While not argued, I add that even on facts most favourable to Webber
Academy, a defence of waiver by the complainants of their human rights would
not be available. It has been well established that human rights are a matter
of public policy, created for the benefit of the community, inherent to the
dignity of every individual, and cannot be waived or contracted out of:
Ontario
(Human Rights Commission) v. Etobicoke (Borough)
,

1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R.
202, at 8 to 9;
Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud
,

1992 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970, paras.
23 to 25
; and
Dickason v. University of Alberta
,

1992 CanLII 30 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 1103, 95 D.L.R. (4th) 439, para.
116
. Further, it is highly
unlikely that waiver would be made out on these facts, even if it was open as a
possible defence.

[
107
]

I therefore conclude that even though the tribunal’s findings on the
pre-enrollment communications and school tour were unreasonable, in law they
could have no effect on whether Webber Academy unlawfully discriminated against
the students. In its proper place, I will address whether my conclusions on the
tribunal’s fact findings have any effect on damages.

X         Expert Evidence of Dr.
Ahmed

[
108
]

Webber Academy also argues that the tribunal
gave inadequate consideration to Dr. Ahmed’s evidence, confining it to the
question of sincerity of belief.

[
109
]

For reasons given earlier, expert evidence of
the content of a body of religious doctrine is of limited relevance when
considering alleged discrimination based on religious beliefs. The tribunal
carefully addressed Dr. Ahmed’s evidence, and gave it the relevance required
under
Amselem
.

[
110
]

Further, Dr. Ahmed’s analysis of the prayer
calendar adds little. While there was some confusion in the evidence about
whether the students would be required to pray during school hours for only
three to four months during the school year, or through the entire school year,
ample evidence indicates that for at least some material portion of the school
year their beliefs required them to pray during school hours.

[
111
]

In my view, the tribunal made no errors in considering
and applying Dr. Ahmed’s evidence.

XI        Damages

[
112
]

The tribunal awarded damages for distress,
injury and loss of dignity in the amount of $12,000 for Mr. Amir and $14,000
for Mr. Siddique. The latter was slightly higher to take into account the tribunal’s
finding that Mr. Siddique had developed problems with persistent fear about
praying on public grounds.

[
113
]

The damages awards are at the high end of the
range for damages given by other human rights tribunals for this head of
damages. However, they are within the range of what has been held acceptable by
tribunals and courts, and therefore intervention would not be warranted on that
basis.

[
114
]

One of the factors the tribunal took into
account was its finding that “these Parents and Students were given the
impression by Webber Academy, in advance of enrollment that something could be
worked out regarding the Students’ prayer requirements,” and Dr. Nazar
testified that if she had known otherwise her son would not have been enrolled
(para 129). For reasons given earlier, the tribunal’s findings on this point
were unreasonable, although I concluded it did not give rise to setting aside
the finding of unlawful discrimination. It remains to consider whether Webber
Academy is entitled to relief regarding the remedy, namely the amount of
damages.

[
115
]

I conclude that the tribunal’s decision on
damages should stand, for two reasons.

[
116
]

First,
Dunsmuir
held that judicial review
“is also concerned with whether the decision falls within a range of possible,
acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law”
(para. 47). We have been reminded that judicial review does not mean that every
element of the reasoning must independently pass a reasonableness test, but
that the focus must be based on the adequacy of both the decision-making
process and the decision itself, as a whole:
Telus
, para. 22 (citing
Law
Society of

New Brunswick v. Ryan
,
2003 SCC 20
, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 247,
para.
56
).

[
117
]

Second, human rights legislation is remedial,
not punitive:
Act
, section 32 (1)(b)(iv) and (v);
North Vancouver
School District No. 44 v. Jubran
,
2005 BCCA 201
, 253 D.L.R. (4
th
)
294, at para.
115
.  Thus, the emphasis must be on how discrimination affected
complainants, not on the blameworthiness of respondents, even though the latter
may be a factor.

[
118
]

I interpret the tribunal’s findings on damages
to have been based mainly on how the students were affected by Webber Academy
forbidding them to pray on campus, which also affected how they felt at the
campus generally and when encountering administration staff. In addition to
feelings of humiliation and embarrassment, they were upset in being unable to
complete their education at the leading academic institution they had chosen.
The tribunal, in my estimation, placed relatively little weight on the
pre-enrollment communications and focused on the compensatory element of
damages. That was the correct approach.

[
119
]

Taking into account the requirement to review
the decision according to the range of possible, acceptable outcomes according
to the facts and the law, I am satisfied that the damages awarded were reasonable.

XII      Conclusions

[
120
]

Webber Academy characterizes the tribunal’s
decision as a “precedent-setting decision with far reaching implications”
(Brief, para. 3). With respect, that is not an accurate characterization.

[
121
]

The tribunal applied well-established principles
of law. For many years, public and private schools have been required to adhere
to human rights legislation in offering their educational services to the
public.  As only one example, in
Sehdev v. Bayview Glen Junior Schools Ltd
.,

1998 Carswell Ont 3315
,
1988 CanLII 8934 (ON HRT)
, 9 C.H.R.R. D/4881 (Ont. Brd. Inq.) a private school
with a strict uniform policy was found to have unlawfully discriminated against
a Sikh student in prohibiting him from wearing a turban, because a slight
liberalization of the dress code would not compromise the school’s objectives.
It did not matter that there were many other schools available to the student
with less strict dress codes. Discrimination is permitted only when reasonable
and justifiable as determined by well-established principles.

[
122
]

Webber Academy, to its credit, adopted a public
policy of welcoming young people of many faiths and cultures, and to exemplify
its policy, published photographs of students with turbans and facial hair even
though these practices contravened usual school policies.

[
123
]

For some reason, it drew the line at Sunni
prayer rituals, conducted in private, in a place that was convenient to the
school and the students from time to time. Its policy thus discriminated
against the belief of the complainant Sunni Muslim students as compared, for
example, to students who overtly averred their religious affiliation by forms
of dress and grooming. There was no demonstrated hardship, let alone undue
hardship, motivating this policy.

[
124
]

For the reasons given, Webber Academy’s appeal
is dismissed.
